label: Q11
title: Perfect competition: everyone is a price-taker
hook: After this lesson you can define a perfectly competitive market, a price-taking producer and consumer, and explain the two conditions (plus free entry and exit) that make a market perfectly competitive.

cards.body:
Imagine the tomato row at Chorsu bazaar. There are 100 sellers. All the tomatoes look the same.

One seller, Dilnoza, wants to ask a higher price. What happens? Buyers just walk to the next table. So she cannot choose her price. She takes the price that everybody else is charging.

The same is true for you as a buyer. If you buy 2 kg or 5 kg, the price of tomatoes does not move. You are too small.

This is the main idea of Week 7: in perfect competition, nobody alone can change the price.

cards.h: So who sets the price? The whole market
cards.body:
Slide 3 says: the price is set by industry demand and industry supply. That is the normal supply-and-demand picture from Week 3, but for all buyers and all sellers together.

In the textbook tomato example (slide 18), all the farms together and all the buyers together give a market price of $18 per bushel, with 500 bushels sold.

chart.caption: Industry demand and industry supply meet at E: the market price is $18. Every farm and every buyer must accept it.

cards.body:
• Price-taking producer: a producer whose actions have no effect on the market price of the good it sells.
  • Price-taking consumer: a consumer whose actions have no effect on the market price of the good he or she buys.
  • Perfectly competitive market: a market where all participants, both consumers and producers, are price-takers.
  • Perfectly competitive industry: an industry where the producers are price-takers.

Small difference to remember: market = buyers and sellers. Industry = only the producers.

For one farm, the market price is just a fixed number. It can sell 1 bushel or 7 bushels, and each bushel brings $18.

  • Ask more than $18: buyers go to other farms, it sells nothing.
  • Ask less than $18: no reason, it can already sell all it wants at $18.

So the firm's demand is a flat (horizontal) line at the market price. Each extra bushel adds exactly $18 to revenue, so marginal revenue = price (MR = P). You will use this line in all the next lessons.

chart.caption: A price-taker can sell any amount at the market price, so its demand line is flat: P = MR.

cards.h: Condition 1: no producer has a large market share
cards.body:
Market share = the fraction of the total industry output that one producer makes.

Market share = (firm's output) ÷ (total industry output)

Example: 100 tomato farms make 500 bushels in total. One farm makes 5 bushels. Its share = 5 ÷ 500 = 1%. If it doubles or stops production, the market hardly notices. So it cannot move the price.

Compare: if one company made 60% of all output, it could cut its output, create a shortage, and push the price up. That company is not a price-taker.

A good is a standardized product, also called a commodity, when consumers see the products of different producers as the same good.

Examples: wheat, tomatoes, raw cotton, potatoes. Wheat from farm A = wheat from farm B. So if farm A asks more, buyers switch at once.

Not standardized: iPhone vs Samsung, Coca-Cola vs Pepsi, Nike shoes. People think these are different, so a brand can charge more and still keep some buyers. Then the firm is not a price-taker.

You need both conditions: many small producers and the same product.

There is free entry and exit when new producers can easily come into an industry, and existing producers can easily leave it.

Example: anyone can rent land and start growing tomatoes; a farmer who loses money can stop next season.

Slide 4 lists it separately from the two necessary conditions. In the textbook it is not strictly necessary, but most perfectly competitive industries have it. It becomes very important in the long run: profits pull new firms in, losses push firms out (later slides 19–24).

example.problem:
A region has 400 wheat farms. Together they grow 80,000 tons of wheat. Farm A grows 200 tons.

  1. What is Farm A's market share?
  2. Is Farm A a price-taker? Why?
  3. In the smartphone industry, Company X sells 30% of all phones. Is this industry perfectly competitive?
example.solution:
1. Market share = 200 ÷ 80,000 = 0.0025 = 0.25%.
  2. Yes. Its share is tiny (condition 1) and wheat is a standardized product (condition 2). If Farm A changes its output, or asks a higher price, the market price does not change; buyers simply buy identical wheat from other farms.
  3. No. Company X has a large market share (30%), and phones are not standardized: buyers see brands as different goods. So Company X can affect the price; it is not a price-taker.

check.q: Define a price-taking consumer.
check.a: A consumer whose actions have no effect on the market price of the good he or she buys.

check.q: What is the formula for market share?
check.a: Firm's output ÷ total industry output.

check.q: Why does a standardized product make a producer a price-taker?
check.a: Buyers see all producers' goods as the same, so if one producer asks a higher price, buyers just buy from another producer.

check.q: In a perfectly competitive market, who sets the price?
check.a: No single person. The price is set by industry demand and industry supply together.

check.q: Is free entry and exit one of the two necessary conditions on slide 4?
check.a: No. It is listed separately. It is a usual feature of perfectly competitive industries, important in the long run.

exam.question: What is a perfectly competitive market? Define a price-taking producer and a price-taking consumer. State the two necessary conditions for perfect competition, and explain free entry and exit.
exam.answer:
A perfectly competitive market is a market in which all participants, both consumers and producers, are price-takers. The price is determined by industry demand and industry supply. An industry where producers are price-takers is a perfectly competitive industry.

A price-taking producer is a producer whose actions have no effect on the market price of the good it sells. A price-taking consumer is a consumer whose actions have no effect on the market price of the good he or she buys.

Two necessary conditions:

  1. No producer has a large market share. Market share is the fraction of total industry output produced by one producer. When every share is small, no producer can change the price by changing its output.
  2. The good is a standardized product (commodity): consumers regard the products of different producers as the same good. So a producer who raises its price loses its buyers to other producers.

Free entry and exit: new producers can easily enter the industry and existing producers can easily leave it. It is typical of perfectly competitive industries (for example, wheat or tomato farming).

memorize: Perfectly competitive market: ALL buyers and sellers are price-takers
Price-taker: own actions have no effect on the market price
Price comes from industry demand + industry supply
Condition 1: no large market share (share = own output ÷ industry output)
Condition 2: standardized product = commodity (all producers' goods seen as the same)
Free entry and exit: easy to come in or leave (listed separately)
Firm sees a flat line: P = MR

label: Q23
title: Keep operating with a loss? The shut-down rule (P vs AVC)
hook: You will be able to use the slide 11 table to decide when a firm should keep producing even while it loses money, and to show why the rule becomes P > AVC.

cards.body:
You run a samsa shop. You signed a rent contract: 1000 per month. You must pay it even if the shop is closed. That is a fixed cost (FC).

Meat, flour, gas and your helper's wage are paid only when you work. That is variable cost (VC). If you close, VC = 0.

This month, sales will not cover all costs. Should you close the shop? Many people say "yes, I am losing money". Economics says: not always.

• Shut down: no sales (TR = 0), no VC, but you still pay FC. Profit = −FC.
  • Operate: profit = TR − VC − FC.

Choose the option with the smaller loss. Operating is better when

TR − VC − FC > −FC, which means TR > VC.

In words: keep working if your revenue pays all of the variable cost. Any extra money helps pay the rent.

FC = 1000 in every case. I added three columns to show the logic.

CaseVCTCTRProfit if operateProfit if shut downTR − VCOperate?
a200030005000+2000−10003000Yes
b3000400040000−10001000Yes
c400050004500−500−1000500Yes
d500060005000−1000−10000Maybe
e600070005500−1500−1000−500No

Look at the column TR − VC: positive → operate, zero → maybe (indifferent), negative → shut down.

Revenue is 4500. It pays all the variable cost (4000). The 500 left over pays part of the rent.

  • Operate: you lose 1000 − 500 = 500.
  • Shut down: you lose the full rent, 1000.

Losing 500 is better than losing 1000, so you keep operating. That is exactly the slide's message: "If you shut down, you will lose more money because of the fixed cost."

Case d: revenue only just pays VC, you lose 1000 either way, so "maybe". Case e: revenue (5500) does not even pay VC (6000); each day open makes the loss bigger, so close.

cards.h: From TR > VC to P > AVC
cards.body:
The slide writes the operating condition as: −(TR − VC − FC) < FC. The left side is the loss from operating. So it says: "operate while your loss is smaller than FC".

  1. Remove the brackets: −TR + VC + FC < FC
  2. Cancel FC: VC < TR
  3. Use TR = P × Q and VC = AVC × Q: AVC × Q < P × Q
  4. Divide by Q: P > AVC

Rule (short run): P > AVC → operate (even with a loss). P = AVC → indifferent. P < AVC → shut down. The lowest point of AVC is called the shut-down price.

This is a short-run rule, because FC exists only in the short run. In the long run the contract ends, nothing is fixed, and a firm that keeps losing money leaves the industry (next lesson).

cards.h: On the graph: a loss the firm accepts
cards.body:
The textbook tomato farm (FC = $14). Its shut-down price is $10, its break-even price is $14. Suppose the price is $12.

  • Best output: P = MC → 3.5 bushels. TR = 12 × 3.5 = $42.
  • ATC = $14.14, so TC = $49.50. Loss = $7.50 (red box).
  • AVC = $10.14 < P = $12, so revenue pays all VC ($35.50) and $6.50 of the $14 FC.
  • Shut down instead: lose the whole FC = $14. So operate: $7.50 < $14.

chart.caption: P = $12 is below min ATC ($14) but above min AVC ($10): the farm loses $7.50, less than the $14 FC it would lose by closing.

cards.h: One picture of the whole rule
cards.body:
For each price, compare the two losses of the tomato farm (always producing where P = MC):

Price$6$8$10$12$14
Loss if operate2419.5147.50
Loss if shut down1414141414

The lines cross at P = $10 = minimum AVC. Below $10: shut down. Above $10: operate.

chart.caption: Left of $10, operating loses more than FC, so shut down. Right of $10, operating loses less, so keep producing.

example.problem:
A small shop has fixed cost FC = 600 per month. At its best output, Q = 100 units, its variable cost is VC = 2000. The market price is P = 23.

  1. Find TR, TC and profit. Should the shop operate or shut down in the short run?
  2. Show the same answer with the rule P > AVC.
  3. The price falls to P = 18 (output and VC stay the same). Now what?
example.solution:
1. TR = 23 × 100 = 2300. TC = 600 + 2000 = 2600. Profit = 2300 − 2600 = −300. If it shuts down, profit = −FC = −600. −300 is better, so operate.
  2. AVC = VC ÷ Q = 2000 ÷ 100 = 20. P = 23 > AVC = 20 → operate. (TR − VC = 300 > 0, and this 300 pays half of the rent.)
  3. TR = 1800 < VC = 2000. Operating: profit = 1800 − 2600 = −800. Shut down: −600. P = 18 < AVC = 20 → shut down. This is like case e on the slide.

check.q: If a firm shuts down in the short run, how much does it lose?
check.a: Exactly its fixed cost (FC), because FC must be paid anyway.

check.q: Case e: why should the firm shut down?
check.a: TR (5500) < VC (6000). Operating loses 1500, shutting down loses only 1000.

check.q: Case d says "Maybe". Why?
check.a: TR = VC = 5000, so the loss is 1000 whether it operates or not: the firm is indifferent.

check.q: P = 12, AVC = 10.14, ATC = 14.14. Profit or loss? Operate?
check.a: P < ATC, so a loss. But P > AVC, so operate in the short run.

check.q: What is the shut-down price?
check.a: The minimum of the AVC curve. Below it, the firm shuts down in the short run.

exam.question: Look at the table on slide 11 (cases a–e, FC = 1000). In case c the firm makes a loss. Should it keep operating? Explain why, say what the firm should do in cases d and e, and show how the business operating condition becomes P > AVC.
exam.answer:
Yes, in case c the firm should keep operating. If it shuts down, it still pays the fixed cost of 1000, so it loses 1000. If it operates, profit = TR − TC = 4500 − 5000 = −500. Losing 500 is better than losing 1000. Revenue (4500) covers all the variable cost (4000), and the remaining 500 covers part of the fixed cost.

Case d: TR = VC = 5000, so the loss is 1000 whether it operates or not: the firm is indifferent ("maybe"). Case e: TR = 5500 < VC = 6000; operating loses 1500, more than the 1000 lost by shutting down, so it should shut down. (Cases a and b: profit 2000 and 0, so operate.)

Operating condition: operate while the loss from operating is smaller than FC:
−(TR − VC − FC) < FC ⇒ VC < TR.
Since TR = P × Q and VC = AVC × Q: AVC × Q < P × Q ⇒ P > AVC.

So in the short run a firm keeps producing as long as the price is above average variable cost, even if it makes a loss. The minimum of AVC is the shut-down price.

memorize: Shut down → still pay FC → loss = FC
Operate if loss < FC ⇔ TR > VC
Divide by Q: P > AVC → operate (short run)
Case c: lose 500 open vs 1000 closed → operate
Case d: TR = VC → maybe; case e: TR < VC → shut down
Shut-down price = minimum AVC

label: Q24
title: Break-even price (min ATC) and shut-down price (min AVC): Table 7-4
hook: You will be able to reproduce Table 7-4: compare the price with min ATC and min AVC, and say what a perfectly competitive firm does in the short run and in the long run.

cards.body:
A firm owner asks two questions, on two time scales:

  1. Short run: "Should I produce today?" The fixed cost must be paid anyway. Only the variable cost matters. → Compare P with minimum AVC.
  2. Long run: "Should I stay in this industry?" In the long run nothing is fixed (contracts end, machines can be sold). The firm must cover all its costs. → Compare P with minimum ATC.

Table 7-4 is just these two comparisons. Top half = profitability (long run). Bottom half = production (short run).

cards.h: Where the two key prices are
cards.body:
The MC curve cuts both U-shaped curves at their lowest points.

  • Break-even price = minimum ATC. At this price, profit = 0. Tomato farm: $14 (at 4 bushels).
  • Shut-down price = minimum AVC. Below it, the firm stops producing. Tomato farm: $10 (at 3 bushels).

The shut-down price is always lower, because ATC = AVC + AFC, so ATC lies above AVC.

chart.caption: MC crosses ATC at its minimum ($14 = break-even price) and AVC at its minimum ($10 = shut-down price).

cards.h: Top half: the profitability condition (P vs min ATC)
cards.body:
PriceResult
P > min ATCFirm profitable. Entry into the industry in the long run.
P = min ATCFirm breaks even. No entry or exit in the long run.
P < min ATCFirm unprofitable. Exit from the industry in the long run.

Why entry and exit? Remember free entry and exit: profit attracts new firms; losses make firms leave. (Profit here means economic profit, so "break even" means the owner earns just a normal return.)

cards.h: Bottom half: the production condition (P vs min AVC)
cards.body:
PriceResult
P > min AVCFirm produces in the short run. If P < min ATC: covers all variable cost and some but not all fixed cost. If P > min ATC: covers all variable and fixed cost.
P = min AVCFirm is indifferent between producing or not. Just covers variable cost.
P < min AVCFirm shuts down in the short run. Does not cover variable cost.

This is the slide 11 rule (P > AVC) written with the lowest point of AVC.

cards.h: Three price zones, with the tomato farm
cards.body:
The farm always chooses output where P = MC. FC = $14.

PriceOutputProfitShort runLong run
$185+$18producenew firms enter
$14 (= min ATC)4$0produceno entry, no exit
$123.5−$7.50produce (loss < FC)exit
$10 (= min AVC)3−$14indifferent (loss = FC)exit
$80−$14shut downexit

The middle zone is the tricky one: between $10 and $14 the firm makes a loss but still produces in the short run, then leaves in the long run. (At $8, producing 2.5 bushels would lose $19.50, more than the $14 FC, so it closes.)

cards.h: Result: the firm's short-run supply curve
cards.body:
Put the rules together (slides 12–13):

  • If it produces, the firm chooses Q where P = MC. So the MC curve tells how much it supplies at each price.
  • But below the shut-down price it produces nothing.

So the short-run individual supply curve = the part of the MC curve above minimum AVC.

Small correction: slide 12 writes "Ps: minimum average cost". It should be minimum average variable cost (the shut-down price), as slide 13 says: "P > AVC".

chart.caption: Supply = MC above the shut-down point (3 bushels, $10). Below $10 the farm supplies zero.

example.problem:
A perfectly competitive firm has minimum AVC = $20 and minimum ATC = $30. For each market price, say (i) profit, break even or loss, (ii) produce or shut down in the short run, (iii) entry, exit or nothing in the long run.

(a) P = $35   (b) P = $30   (c) P = $25   (d) P = $15
example.solution:
• (a) $35 > min ATC: profit; produce; new firms enter in the long run.
  • (b) $30 = min ATC: break even (zero economic profit); produce; no entry or exit.
  • (c) $25: below min ATC ($30) but above min AVC ($20): loss, but still produce in the short run (covers all VC and part of FC); exit in the long run.
  • (d) $15 < min AVC: cannot even cover VC, so shut down now (loss = FC); exit in the long run.

check.q: Break-even price = the minimum of which curve?
check.a: Average total cost (ATC).

check.q: Shut-down price = the minimum of which curve?
check.a: Average variable cost (AVC).

check.q: Which comparison decides entry and exit in the long run?
check.a: P compared with min ATC (the profitability condition).

check.q: min AVC < P < min ATC. What happens?
check.a: Loss, but the firm produces in the short run (covers VC and part of FC); in the long run it exits.

check.q: What is the firm's short-run supply curve?
check.a: The part of its MC curve above minimum AVC (the shut-down price).

exam.question: Summarize the perfectly competitive firm's profitability and production conditions (Table 7-4). What are the break-even price and the shut-down price? What does the firm do in the short run and in the long run when P is greater than, equal to, or less than each of them?
exam.answer:
The break-even price is the firm's minimum average total cost: at this price economic profit is zero. The shut-down price is its minimum average variable cost.

Profitability condition (P vs min ATC), long run:

  • P > min ATC: the firm is profitable; new firms enter the industry in the long run.
  • P = min ATC: the firm breaks even; no entry into or exit from the industry.
  • P < min ATC: the firm is unprofitable; firms exit the industry in the long run.

Production condition (P vs min AVC), short run:

  • P > min AVC: the firm produces. If P < min ATC, it covers its variable cost and some but not all of its fixed cost; if P > min ATC, it covers all variable and fixed cost.
  • P = min AVC: the firm is indifferent between producing and not; it just covers variable cost.
  • P < min AVC: the firm shuts down in the short run; it does not cover variable cost.

Reason: in the short run fixed cost must be paid anyway, so the firm only needs P > AVC to produce. In the long run all costs can be avoided, so it stays only if P covers ATC. Therefore the firm's short-run supply curve is its MC curve above minimum AVC.

memorize: Break-even price = min ATC → profit or loss → entry/exit (LONG run)
Shut-down price = min AVC → produce or not (SHORT run)
MC cuts ATC and AVC at their minimums
P > min ATC: profit, entry. P = min ATC: zero profit, no entry/exit. P < min ATC: exit
min AVC < P < min ATC: loss but produce now, exit later
P < min AVC: shut down (loss = FC)
SR supply = MC above min AVC

label: Q12
title: Short-run industry supply curve and short-run market equilibrium
hook: You will be able to define the short-run industry supply curve and short-run market equilibrium, build industry supply by adding firms' quantities, and explain the tomato example (Figure 7-5).

cards.h: From one farm to the whole industry
cards.body:
Last lesson: each firm's supply curve is its MC curve above minimum AVC. Now we want the supply of all firms together.

The industry supply curve shows the relationship between the price of a good and the total output of the industry (slide 16).

How to build it: pick a price, ask every firm "how much do you sell at this price?", and add the quantities: Q = q1 + q2 + … + qk. Repeat for other prices.

We add sideways (quantities), never prices. This is called horizontal summation.

chart.caption: At P = $16, firm B sells 3 and firm A sells 6, so the industry sells 3 + 6 = 9.

cards.body:
The short-run industry supply curve shows how the quantity supplied by an industry depends on the market price, given a fixed number of producers.

"Short run" = there is no time for new firms to build farms, or for old firms to sell everything and leave. So the number of producers is fixed.

It slopes upward: when the price rises, every firm moves up its own MC curve and produces more, so the total rises.

There are 100 identical farms. Each farm is the farm from the last lessons: shut-down price $10, and it supplies where P = MC.

PriceOne farm suppliesIndustry (× 100)
below $1000
$103300
$144400
$185500
$226600

So the industry curve starts at (300 bushels, $10). Below $10, no farm wants to produce, so the industry supplies nothing.

There is a short-run market equilibrium when the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded, taking the number of producers as given.

In Figure 7-5 the short-run industry supply curve meets demand at EMKT: price $18, quantity 500 bushels. Each of the 100 farms sells 5 bushels.

chart.caption: Figure 7-5 (demand drawn approximately): supply starts at the shut-down price $10 (300 bushels) and meets demand at $18, 500 bushels.

cards.body:
At $18 each farm earns a profit: (18 − 14.40) × 5 = $18 (slide 9). Profit attracts new farms. But along the short-run curve the number of farms is fixed, so this cannot happen yet.

In the long run (slides 19–22) new farms enter, the supply curve shifts right, and the price falls until it reaches the break-even price, $14 (zero profit). That is the long-run equilibrium.

Exam key words: short run = fixed number of producers; long run = entry and exit allowed.

example.problem:
An industry has 100 identical firms. One firm supplies 0 units if P < $10, and 3, 4, 5, 6 units at P = $10, $14, $18, $22. Market demand is: $10 → 900, $14 → 700, $18 → 500, $22 → 300 units.

  1. Build the short-run industry supply schedule.
  2. Find the short-run market equilibrium.
  3. What is assumed about the number of firms?
example.solution:
1. Multiply each firm's quantity by 100: $10 → 300, $14 → 400, $18 → 500, $22 → 600 (and 0 below $10).
  2. Compare: at $14, Qd = 700 > Qs = 400 (shortage, price rises). At $22, Qs = 600 > Qd = 300 (surplus, price falls). At $18, Qs = Qd = 500. Equilibrium: P = $18, Q = 500; each firm sells 5.
  3. The number of firms is fixed at 100. That is what makes it a short-run supply curve and a short-run equilibrium.

check.q: What is held fixed along the short-run industry supply curve?
check.a: The number of producers.

check.q: Do we add prices or quantities to get industry supply?
check.a: Quantities: at each price, Q = q<sub>1</sub> + q<sub>2</sub> + … + q<sub>k</sub> (horizontal summation).

check.q: In Figure 7-5, why is there no supply below $10?
check.a: $10 is the shut-down price (min AVC). Below it, every farm shuts down.

check.q: Define short-run market equilibrium.
check.a: Quantity supplied = quantity demanded, taking the number of producers as given.

check.q: At E<sub>MKT</sub> ($18) farms earn profit. Is this a long-run equilibrium?
check.a: No. Profit attracts entry; supply shifts right and the price falls toward the break-even price ($14).

exam.question: What is the short-run industry supply curve? What is a short-run market equilibrium? Explain how the industry supply curve is related to the supply curves of individual firms.
exam.answer:
The short-run industry supply curve shows how the quantity supplied by an industry depends on the market price, given a fixed number of producers.

It is built from the individual supply curves: each firm supplies along its MC curve above minimum AVC, and at each price the quantities of all firms are added: Q = q1 + q2 + … + qk. As the price rises, each firm produces more, so the industry curve slopes upward. Below the shut-down price no firm produces.

A short-run market equilibrium exists when the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded, taking the number of producers as given.

Example (Figure 7-5): 100 tomato farms; below the shut-down price of $10 no farm produces. The short-run industry supply curve meets demand at $18 and 500 bushels (5 bushels per farm). It is "short run" because the number of producers cannot change; in the long run firms can enter or exit.

memorize: SR industry supply: industry Q vs price, FIXED number of producers
Built by adding firms' quantities at each price (horizontal sum)
Each firm: MC above min AVC; below shut-down price, 0
SR market equilibrium: Qs = Qd, number of producers given
Fig 7-5: 100 farms, shut-down $10 (300 bushels), equilibrium $18 and 500 bushels
Long run: entry/exit, price goes to break-even ($14)
